You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
The failing test case `testIteratorSequenceBreaking()` checks that multiple iterators created by repeated calls to `CSVParser.iterator()` on the same parser instance correctly continue reading from the sequence of CSV records without losing or skipping records. The test includes scenarios with breaking out of the iterator loop and then resuming reading from a new iterator as well as using enhanced for-loops which also rely on the iterable interface.

From inspecting the code for `CSVParser.iterator()`, the iterator returned is an anonymous inner class that keeps track of a single `current` cached record for peeking on `hasNext()`. The important point is that each call to `iterator()` creates a new independent Iterator instance but internally they all call the same underlying `CSVParser.nextRecord()` method to get the next record from the shared parser state.

The method `CSVParser.nextRecord()` accesses the shared lexer to get tokens for the next CSV record and advance state accordingly. Because this parser uses a shared lexer that moves forward as tokens are read, creating multiple iterators does not create independent streams. Instead, all iterators are linked to the same lexer state.

The key problem arises because each new iterator "owns" a `current` cached peeked record independently. When a new iterator is created, its internal `current` is `null`. On the first call to `hasNext()` for that new iterator, the call to `getNextRecord()` consumes the shared lexer stream by a call to `nextRecord()`. This reads and consumes the next record from the underlying lexer. Because the lexer is shared, that record is "consumed" and cannot be revisited by any other iterator. This causes records to be effectively skipped or lost when switching iterators.

The test failures and bug report mentioning "Repeated calls to CSVParser Iterable return new Iterators that each reference the same underlying parser lexer" and the fact that consumption by one iterator's `hasNext()` call cannot be accessed by subsequent newly created iterators demonstrates this issue exactly.

Hence the root cause is that the `iterator()` implementation returns completely new iterator instances each reading from the same underlying cursor in the shared lexer, but does not coordinate or share peeked records or cursor position among them. This leads to record consumption upon peeking by a new iterator which then causes records to be lost to others.

This diagnosis explains why consecutive iterators or for-each loops (which call `iterator()` internally) will break the sequence and skip records after any peeking (`hasNext()`) call on a new iterator.

In summary, the bug occurs because multiple iterators returned from a single `CSVParser` instance are not independent streams but share mutable lexer state without synchronization or coordination of peeked records, leading to lost records during sneaky peek operations on newly created iterators.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
